paragraphs.heading: A radio observatory in the desert
paragraphs.text: The Jansky Very Large Array, or VLA, is an observatory in the southwestern United States that studies the sky at centimetre radio wavelengths. Built in the 1970s, it sits on the Plains of San Agustin in central New Mexico, about 80 kilometres west of Socorro, at an elevation of 2,120 metres. It is part of the National Radio Astronomy Observatory, a National Science Foundation facility run by Associated Universities, Inc.

paragraphs.heading: Many dishes acting as one
paragraphs.text: The VLA has 28 dish antennas, each 25 metres across and weighing 209 metric tons. At any moment 27 are in use while the remaining one rotates through maintenance. The dishes stand along three arms laid out in a Y shape, and each arm is 21 kilometres long. Together with the equipment and computers behind them, they work as an interferometer, so that the whole array behaves in essence like a single antenna whose diameter can change.

paragraphs.heading: Dishes on rails
paragraphs.text: Every dish rides on double parallel railway tracks, and a specially built lifting locomotive can carry it to one of many prepared spots; at one point the tracks even cross U.S. Route 60. Spreading the dishes out or pulling them in shifts the balance between the array's angular resolution and its sensitivity to surface brightness. Its angular resolution can reach between 0.2 and 0.04 arcseconds. There are four common layouts, from A, the widest, to D, the tightest, in which every dish is within 600 metres of the centre. The observatory normally cycles through all its layouts every 16 months, moving the antennas every three to four months.

paragraphs.heading: What it looks at
paragraphs.text: The VLA was designed as an all-round instrument for many kinds of objects, from radio galaxies, quasars and pulsars to supernova remnants, the Sun and planets, black holes, and hydrogen gas in our galaxy and others. Astronomers using it have made key observations of black holes and of protoplanetary disks around young stars. They have also found magnetic filaments and traced complex gas motions at the centre of the Milky Way. In 1989 it was even used to receive radio transmissions from the Voyager 2 spacecraft as it passed Neptune.

paragraphs.heading: Mapping the radio sky
paragraphs.text: The VLA has carried out several big radio surveys of the sky, among them the NRAO VLA Sky Survey. A newer one, the VLA Sky Survey, began in September 2017 and aims to cover all the sky the VLA can see, 80% of Earth's sky, in three full scans. Astronomers expect it to reveal about 10 million new objects, four times more than are currently known. Between December 2014 and January 2015 the array also scanned the galaxies M31 and M32, quickly checking trillions of systems for very powerful signals from advanced civilizations.

paragraphs.heading: Building and upgrading
paragraphs.text: The first antenna was installed in September 1975, and the whole complex had its formal opening in 1980, having cost $78.5 million in all. No other set of radio telescopes on Earth was bigger. Starting in 2001, an upgrade called the Expanded Very Large Array swapped the 1970s electronics for modern equipment and improved the instrument's sensitivity, frequency range and resolution. The decade-long project finished on time and on budget in 2012, raising the array's technical abilities by factors of up to 8,000. On March 31, 2012, the array was officially renamed at a ceremony inside its Antenna Assembly Building.

paragraphs.heading: The next generation
paragraphs.text: In June 2023 the National Radio Astronomy Observatory announced plans to replace the ageing antennas with 160 new ones on the site, plus 100 more spread across North America. Building it is estimated at about $2 billion, with running costs of around $90 million. It will greatly expand what the site can do and raise its frequency sensitivity from 50 GHz to more than 100 GHz. The new facility will be called the Next Generation Very Large Array, or ngVLA.
